title: Fahrenheit and Celsius
blurb: Convert any temperature between Celsius and Fahrenheit with the steps in the right order, compare readings on different scales, and convert a change in temperature.
question: A child's temperature is 39 °C, and the parent's thermometer reads in °F. What should the parent's thermometer show, and how would 102.2 °F be written in °C?

teach.body: Formally, the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales differ in two ways: their zero points (water freezes at 0 °C but at 32 °F) and the size of one degree (100 Celsius degrees span the same range as 180 Fahrenheit degrees, so 1 °C = 9/5 = 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees). In plain English: to convert you must both stretch (× 9/5 or × 5/9) and shift (+ 32 or - 32), and you must do them in the right order.

teach.caption: Each formula undoes the other in reverse order, like putting on and taking off shoes and socks.

teach.h: Multiply then add; subtract then multiply
teach.body: Celsius to Fahrenheit: °F = (9/5 × °C) + 32. Multiply first, then add 32. Fahrenheit to Celsius: °C = (°F - 32) × 5/9. Subtract 32 first, then multiply. On a basic calculator, 9/5 is 1.8: multiply by 1.8 going to °F, and divide by 1.8 going to °C (dividing by 1.8 is the same as multiplying by 5/9). Round only at the very end.

teach.caption: Use these to sense-check: any reading above -40 is a bigger number in °F than in °C.

items: 100 °F to °C, to the nearest tenth: 100 - 32 = 68. 68 ÷ 1.8 = 37.77..., which rounds to 37.8 °C.
Comparing 38.2 °C with 100.6 °F: 38.2 × 1.8 + 32 = 100.76 °F, so 38.2 °C is the higher reading.

teach.caption: A straight line: each 1 °C step is 1.8 °F. The scales cross at -40, where -40 °C = -40 °F.

a bigger number of Fahrenheit degrees

teach.caption: For a CHANGE in temperature, multiply by 1.8 or 5/9 but never add or subtract 32: the 32 only shifts actual readings.

teach.body: Sofia, a medical assistant applying to an RN program, reads a child's temperature as 39.0 °C, but the parent asks for Fahrenheit. Multiply by 9/5: 39.0 × 1.8 = 70.2. Add 32: 70.2 + 32 = 102.2 °F. An hour later the fever has fallen by 1.5 °C. That is a change, so no 32: 1.5 × 1.8 = 2.7 °F, and the new reading is 102.2 - 2.7 = 99.5 °F.

teach.text: The exam's favorite wrong answers: forgetting the 32, adding 32 before multiplying (°C to °F), multiplying before subtracting 32 (°F to °C), using 5/9 where 9/5 belongs, and rounding 5/9 or the reading too early. For a change in temperature, adding or subtracting 32 is itself the trap.

items: A change of 1 °C = a change of 1.8 °F; no 32 for changes.
To compare readings on different scales, convert them all to one scale first.

summary: You can now convert any reading between Celsius and Fahrenheit by doing the steps in the correct order, and sense-check it against anchor values. You can also compare readings on different scales and convert a change in temperature without the 32.

A.q: A room thermometer reads 22 °C. What is the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 1.8 but forgets to add 32.

A.q: A patient's temperature is 38 °C. What is the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit?

whyNot.1: This multiplies by 1.8 but forgets to add 32.

A.q: A patient's temperature is 96.8 °F. What is the temperature in degrees Celsius?

whyNot.1: This multiplies by 5/9 first and subtracts 32 afterward.
whyNot.3: This subtracts 32 but then multiplies by 9/5 instead of 5/9.

B.q: A thermometer reads 102.2 °F. What is this temperature in degrees Celsius?

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 5/9 without subtracting 32 first.
whyNot.1: This multiplies by 5/9 first and subtracts 32 afterward: the steps are in the wrong order.
whyNot.2: This subtracts 32 but then multiplies by 9/5 instead of 5/9.

B.q: A patient's temperature rises by 2 °C. By how many degrees Fahrenheit does it rise?
B.why: A change of 1 °C equals 1.8 °F, so 2 × 1.8 = 3.6 °F. No 32 for a change.

whyNot.0: This multiplies the change by 5/9 instead of 9/5.
whyNot.1: This keeps the Celsius number; Fahrenheit degrees are smaller, so the number must be larger.
whyNot.3: This adds 32 to a change; the 32 only shifts actual readings.

B.q: Which pair shows the same temperature on both scales?

whyNot.3: This adds 32 before multiplying: (10 + 32) × 1.8. In fact 10 °C = 50 °F.

C.q: Which temperature reading is the lowest?
C.why: Change all to °F: 36.5 °C = 97.7 °F; 97.3 °F; 36.4 °C = 97.52 °F; 97.9 °F. The lowest is 97.3 °F (about 36.3 °C).

whyNot.3: 97.9 °F is the highest of the four readings (about 36.6 °C).

C.q: A patient's temperature rises from 98.6 °F to 101.3 °F. What is the new temperature in degrees Celsius?

whyNot.0: This adds the 2.7 degree Fahrenheit rise straight onto 37 °C; Fahrenheit and Celsius degrees are different sizes.
whyNot.2: This multiplies by 5/9 first and then subtracts 32.

C.q: A medication refrigerator reads 45 °F. What is this temperature in degrees Celsius, to the nearest tenth?

whyNot.1: This subtracts 32 but never multiplies by 5/9.
whyNot.2: This subtracts 32 and then multiplies by 9/5 instead of 5/9.
whyNot.3: This multiplies 45 by 5/9 without subtracting 32 first.

reteach.title: Think of a thermostat with two dials
reteach.question: Picture a thermostat whose two dials are labeled differently but always point to the same temperature. Why do you need two steps, in a set order, to read one dial from the other?

blocks.h: Different starting points, different step sizes
blocks.body: The Fahrenheit dial starts its count 32 degrees higher (water freezes at 32 °F, not 0) and its degrees are smaller: 9 Fahrenheit degrees fit into every 5 Celsius degrees. So to read °F from °C, stretch by 9/5, then shift up 32. To go back, undo in reverse: shift down 32 first, then shrink by 5/9. Like getting dressed and undressed, the last step on the way in is the first step on the way out.

blocks.text: If your Celsius answer is bigger than the Fahrenheit reading you started with (for anything above -40), you skipped or misplaced the 32.

whyNot.0: This multiplies by 1.8 but forgets to add 32.
whyNot.1: This adds 32 but skips the multiplication by 9/5.
whyNot.2: This uses the °F to °C formula on a Celsius reading.

explain.body: Subtract 32 FIRST, then multiply by 5/9. 77 °F: 77 - 32 = 45, and 45 × 5 ÷ 9 = 25 °C.

whyNot.1: This subtracts 32 but then multiplies by 9/5 instead of 5/9.
whyNot.3: This multiplies by 5/9 first and then subtracts 32.

explain.body: Water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F and boils at 100 °C = 212 °F (at sea level). The scales meet at -40 °C = -40 °F. Check any answer against the nearest anchor.

test.q: Which pair shows the same temperature on both scales?

whyNot.0: 0 °C is 32 °F, the freezing point of water.
whyNot.2: This multiplies 100 by 1.8 but leaves out the 32: 100 °C = 212 °F.
whyNot.3: This reverses the freezing point: 0 °C = 32 °F, and 32 °C = 89.6 °F.

explain.body: A rise or fall is a difference, so the 32 cancels out. Celsius change × 1.8 = Fahrenheit change; Fahrenheit change × 5/9 = Celsius change.

test.q: A fever falls by 4.5 °F. By how many degrees Celsius has it fallen?
test.why: 4.5 × 5/9 = 2.5 °C. No 32, because this is a change, not a reading.

whyNot.2: This keeps the Fahrenheit number; Celsius degrees are larger, so the number must be smaller.
